title: Held-apart body-mass, fat and lean trajectories under over- and underfeeding and fasting (task 5563, LN-5 {R-STORES})
source: Abstracts, article pages and PDFs listed in sources.json under ST-* keys. Where a page returned a browser check, an HTTP error or a scan, the Note says relayed and names the search result the figure came from. A null Value, Low and High means no opened page gave the figure. Rows marked derived are my arithmetic. Task 5563, LN-5.
rows: 36 men enrolled (32 analysed by Dulloo); table relayed from the UNU text

Relayed from a search summary of the UNU table (the page returned HTTP 503), 'about 70 kg'; cites Keys 1950 Tables 181 and 457. Fat 9.9 kg and FFM 60.1 kg at control (9.9 + 60.1 = 70.0, derived check).
Body weight after 24 weeks of semistarvation
Relayed. Loss 16.8 kg = 24% of 70 kg (derived); Kalm and Semba say 'most lost more than 25%', so the mean sits just under that line. Fat 3.3 kg and FFM 49.9 kg (53.2 = 3.3 + 49.9).
Body fat lost in 24 weeks of semistarvation

Derived: 9.9 - 3.3. Fat-free mass lost 10.2 kg. In mass terms 39% fat and 61% fat-free; in energy terms (39.5 and 7.6 MJ/kg) fat 260.7 MJ and fat-free 77.5 MJ, a lean share of 23% (derived). The Hall p-ratio p = 2.0/(2.0 + F) is 0.17 at F = 9.9 kg and 0.38 at F = 3.3 kg (derived), so the observed share lies inside the model's range. Not independent for Hall's parameters: Hall 2006 fitted a few parameters to this experiment.
Men followed from baseline through 24 weeks of semistarvation and 12 weeks of restricted refeeding
Minnesota experiment reanalysis of individual data

Abstract: large individual variation in protein/fat partition; initial body fat the strongest predictor; BMR adjusted for composition fell in proportion to fat regained. No weight or fat figures on the abstract (PubMed page opened). Weekly weights and body composition are in Keys 1950, not found online in this unit.
Correlation of total hyperphagic response with fat recovery
12 starved and refed men: 12 weeks restricted then 8 weeks ad libitum refeeding
With FFM recovery r = -0.5. A feedback from body composition to intake; relevant to LN-6, not to the store identity.
Mean weight gain from 84,000 kcal of overfeeding
12 pairs of identical young men; +1,000 kcal/d, 6 days a week, 84 of 100 days; 353 MJ extra each

353 MJ / 8.1 kg = 43.6 MJ per kg gained (derived), above the 39.5 MJ/kg of fat, so extra expenditure and lean gain are in the answer. Range is across individuals; within-pair similarity about 3 times between-pair variance.
Share of the rise in daily expenditure due to NEAT under 1,000 kcal/d overfeeding

'Two-thirds'. Fat storage varied 10-fold between people; correlation of NEAT change with resistance to fat gain r = 0.77. No kg figure on the abstract (Value for weight gain null: Europe PMC abstract searched).
Weight gain over 8 weeks of overeating, normal-protein diet
25 healthy adults 18 to 35 y, BMI 19 to 30, inpatient, +954 kcal/d (95% CI 884 to 1022); 95% CI as range
Low protein 3.16 kg (1.88 to 4.44), high 6.51 kg (5.23 to 7.79). Extra energy 954 kcal/d x 56 d = 53,424 kcal (derived), which is 8,830 kcal per kg of the normal-protein gain (derived).
Lean body mass gain over 8 weeks of overeating, normal-protein diet

High-protein 3.18 kg (2.37 to 3.98). So 47% of the normal-protein weight gain was lean mass (derived, 2.87/6.05). 50% to over 90% of stored excess energy was fat by the abstract. Resting expenditure rose 160 kcal/d (102 to 218) normal and 227 (165 to 289) high protein.
Weight change in 12 days of calorimeter overfeeding
3 lean men overfed (underfed 3 men: -3.18 kg); carbohydrate intake 540 vs 83 g/d

Relayed from a search result quoting the abstract. Expenditure +6.2% overfed and -10.5% underfed; close to energy balance by day 5; carbohydrate oxidation followed carbohydrate intake closely. Per-day trajectories are in the full paper (not opened).
Body fat loss rate, 6 days of carbohydrate restriction
19 adults with obesity in a metabolic chamber, isocaloric crossover, 5 days baseline
+/- 6 as printed, SD or SEM not stated; fat restriction 89 +/- 6 g/d, p = 0.002. Daily glycogen and water changes are not on the abstract, so this validates fat only.
Lower daily energy intake on the low-fat vs ketogenic diet over 2 weeks
+/- 73 as printed. The abstract does not report weight or fat change (Value for those null; Europe PMC abstract searched; full text not opened), so it adds no store trajectory here.
Increase in 14-day average energy expenditure after the switch to a ketogenic diet
Overweight or obese men, 14-day DLW with 4 days in chambers (secondary analysis)

+/- 63 as printed, P = 0.03. Non-chamber expenditure +203 +/- 89 and +283 +/- 116 kcal/d by two approaches; shows DLW and chamber values disagree on the same diet change, a bound on how tightly expenditure can be validated.
Minimal fat oxidation late in a 21-day fast
+/- 0.21 as printed (2.98 +/- 0.15 per kg FFM). Minimal amino acid oxidation 0.27 +/- 0.08 g/kg/d and glucose oxidation 0.34 +/- 0.14 g/kg/d; amino acids supplied 7% of energy requirement late.
Minimal amino acid oxidation late in a 21-day fast
+/- 0.08 as printed. Obese subjects, so protein sparing here is not a lean-subject value.
Body-weight trajectories of 30-day fasts used to validate the Hall Lancet model

Null. The article text read names the datasets but the figure values were not in the first 100,000 characters; the Stewart and Fleming 1973 (382-day fast) and Kerndt 1982 abstracts on Europe PMC carry no figures, Cahill 1968 is a scanned PDF. A tabulated fasting trajectory is therefore not recorded in this unit.
Participants per CALERIE arm used for validation
overweight men and women per arm
25% restriction for 6 months; 12.5% restriction plus exercise; 3.7 MJ/d liquid diet for 3 months then maintenance
Half-time of the bodyweight response to a change in energy intake
Adults, model (95% of the change in about 3 years)
Model result, not an observation: 'half times of about 1 year'. Its slope assumption: 100 kJ/kg/day (model) vs 94 +/- 6 kJ/kg/day (regression of cross-sectional data).
Energy deficit per kg of weight lost in the 3,500 kcal/lb rule
Rule of thumb; obese subjects with more than about 30 kg initial fat

The model predicts a smaller cumulative deficit per kg for people with less initial fat and for larger losses, because more of the loss is lean tissue; published data from obese and lean subjects are said to support it (abstract; data not read).
Predicted time for fat mass to return to within 5% of its start after semistarvation and refeeding
Hall 2006 model prediction, not an observation
Abstract wording: 'more than one additional year'. A model output; held here only so a later unit can find an observation to test it against.
Peak-to-trough size of the weekly body-weight rhythm
80 adults, BMI 20.0 to 33.5, 4,657 weights measured after waking and before breakfast

Null. The Karger full text gives the pattern (highest Sunday and Monday, lowest Friday; weight losers' weekly maximum on Sunday or Monday in 59% of cases) and linear day-of-week slopes of -0.0004 to -0.0006 with no units stated, but no amplitude in kg or %. Day-to-day weight scatter is therefore unquantified here.
Weekly body weight and fat mass across the 24-week semistarvation phase

Null. Searched: UNU table (start and end only, relayed), Dulloo 1996 and 1997 and 2021 abstracts and Kalm and Semba 2005 (no weekly figures), a Hall model comparison (figures not in the abstract). Keys 1950 Tables 181 and 457 are the stated origin and were not found online.
